newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Bosnian deal done, Holbrooke leans on Milosevic.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian deal done, Holbrooke leans on Milosevic.

text.p: U.S. envoy Richard Holbrooke pressed Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic on Friday to hold up his end of the Dayton peace treaty unless he wanted his country to sink into economic oblivion.

Holbrooke and Milosevic, both adroit and ruthless players in international negotiations, matched wits for 3 1/2 hours before agreeing to an unscheduled extension of their talks on Saturday morning, hinting at a possible breakthrough.
"The discussions (with Milosevic) were intense as always," Holbrooke told reporters as he entered his hotel afterwards.

"It would not be fair to disclose anything (more) at this time," added Holbrooke, the architect of the 1995 Dayton peace treaty between Bosnia's Serb, Croat and Moslem leaders and the patrons of the first two in Yugoslavia and Croatia.
Belgrade analysts said the fact that the talks were to be continued on Saturday raised expectations of major results.

Holbrooke flew into Belgrade on Friday fresh from having resolved a row between Bosnia's ethnic leaders over diplomatic posts which had triggered a punitive international cut-off of contacts with Bosnian ambassadors.
Under the deal, a Moslem will be the Bosnian ambassador to the United Nations, a Serb will be ambassador to Washington and a Croat will be envoy to Japan, according to Holbrooke.
Holbrooke had come out of self-imposed "retirement" from the diplomatic service for the second time in a year to salvage key aspects of the peace treaty he engineered.

Members of Bosnia's multi-ethnic collective presidency also agreed on the composition of a joint military commission and on a single area code for Bosnia's telephone network to support a reintegration of the country envisaged by the peace pact.

"These agreements are full evidence of Western determination (to enforce the peace agreement)," Holbrooke told reporters after the agreement reached in Sarajevo. "These are steps forward and pretty solid ones."

"We got a very good agreement on paper. Compliance is lagging behind, although the last three days have certainly seen a dramatic acceleration of the effort," he told Radio B92 in an interview in Belgrade before meeting Milosevic.
Holbrooke refused to reveal the subject of his talks with Milosevic over dinner in the sprawling White Court palace, the Serbian leader's new residence as president of Yugoslavia.

Diplomats expected Holbrooke to threaten Milosevic with economic sanctions unless he abided by his Dayton commitments, which include delivering his ex-protege, indicted war criminal and former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic, and other Serbs wanted for trial by a U.N. tribunal in The Hague.
"Holbrooke is bringing a bagful of carrots and sticks. It's up to Milosevic to choose which he would rather have," one said.

Milosevic also faced tough questioning about Serbia's handling of human rights in its mostly-Albanian populated province of Kosovo, freedom of the media in Serbia and the slow pace of democratic and economic reforms.
But Holbrooke bemoaned a notion by a part of Serbian opposition to boycott the September 21 presidential and parliamentary elections on the grounds they would be unfair.
"We support the election process. We support Dayton, and I don't think parties that boycott elections do anything but damage themselves. It's stupid to boycott the election."

The diplomats said time and money were running out for the sanctions-battered Yugoslav economy as the government struggled hard to maintain order and feed the 11-million population, a third of which is living in poverty.

"It pains us to see this happening - we don't want to do it (impose new sanctions)," the current U.S. envoy for former Yugoslavia, Robert Gelbard, said. He stressed the United States had "enormous sympathy" for the people of Yugoslavia.
One of the major obstacles to dismantling sanctions was Milosevic's reluctance to implement a deal struck last year which stipulated that Karadzic was to stay out of politics.
A year later, Karadzic and his allies in the Serb-controlled half of Bosnia persist in attempting to circumvent the accords and undermine his successor as Bosnian Serb president, Biljana Plavsic.
She has accused them of plundering Serb territory through vast smuggling rackets and making it their fiefdom.
Plavsic was thrown out of the Serb ruling party and Karadzic loyalists in their Pale stronghold are trying to impeach her.
On his way to Belgrade, Holbrooke flew to the north Bosnian town of Banja Luka to show support for Plavsic.
Gelbard blasted Karadzic's loyalists over their isolationism which had compounded the poverty and decay wrought by the 43-month-long, Serb-Moslem-Croat war in Bosnia.
He said the United States expected Milosevic to intervene.
"President Milosevic is an important person in this region. We have high expectation, knowing that he is a man who has great persuasive powers," Gelbard said.
